1.q: שִׁמְע֤וּ אִיִּים֙ אֵלַ֔⁠י וְ⁠הַקְשִׁ֥יבוּ לְאֻמִּ֖ים מֵ⁠רָח֑וֹק
1.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully to me, coastlands and peoples from far away]

Isaiah is using the **coastlands**, the lands at the edge of the sea, to represent all of the territory between him and those lands. He is using the territory itself to represent the people who live in it. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Listen to me, people throughout the world] or [Listen to me, anyone who can hear me]

Isaiah is using **called me from the womb** as a common expression of the culture to mean “chose me before I was born.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [chose me before I was born]

The expression **he made one remember my name** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [he caused people to remember my name]

2.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a sharp sword** is powerful and effective, so is the message Isaiah speaks with his **mouth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [my mouth powerful and effective]

Here, **mouth** represents “the words that the servant speaks.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words I speak]

Here Isaiah is speaking of Yahweh’s protection as if it were **the shadow of his hand** in which he could be concealed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he protected me with his power]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if he himself were **a polished arrow** that Yahweh had prepared. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And he carefully prepared me for his work]

Here Isaiah is speaking as if he himself were an arrow that Yahweh kept ready **in his quiver**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he kept me in readiness until the time he needed me]

3.note: The term **said** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

4.note: The pronoun **I** refers to the servant, who is the one speaking in this passage. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [But I, the servant, said]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **worthlessness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for nothing worthwhile]

The terms **nothingness** and **vapor** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [for absolutely nothing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **nothingness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what was worthless]

The servant is not using this possessive form **my God** to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [my God, the one I worship]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Yet what is due to me is in the Lord’s control]

5.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה יֹצְרִ֤⁠י מִ⁠בֶּ֨טֶן֙ לְ⁠עֶ֣בֶד ל֔⁠וֹ לְ⁠שׁוֹבֵ֤ב יַֽעֲקֹב֙ אֵלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לא יֵאָסֵ֑ף וְ⁠אֶכָּבֵד֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וֵ⁠אלֹהַ֖⁠י הָיָ֥ה עֻזִּֽ⁠י
5.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about what Yahweh said together with the statement that **Yahweh has said** it, rather than after the descriptions that come in between. Alternate translation: [And now Yahweh has said—the one having formed me from the womb as a servant for him, to return Jacob to him and that Israel would be assembled to him, and I am honored in the eyes of Yahweh, and my God has become my strength—Yahweh has spoken]

The expression **Israel would be assembled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and that God would gather Israel to him]

Isaiah is using **the one having formed me from the womb** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who formed me before I was born.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who formed me before my birth]

The servant is using **in the eyes of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of” or “in the opinion of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the opinion of Yahweh]

Here the servant is speaking of Yahweh as if Yahweh were his **strength**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and my God is the one who makes me strong]

Isaiah is not using this possessive form, **my God**, to indicate that he possesses or controls Yahweh. Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom he worships. Alternate translation: [the God I worship]

5.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה יֹצְרִ֤⁠י מִ⁠בֶּ֨טֶן֙ לְ⁠עֶ֣בֶד ל֔⁠וֹ לְ⁠שׁוֹבֵ֤ב יַֽעֲקֹב֙ אֵלָ֔י⁠ו וְ⁠יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לא יֵאָסֵ֑ף וְ⁠אֶכָּבֵד֙ בְּ⁠עֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וֵ⁠אלֹהַ֖⁠י הָיָ֥ה עֻזִּֽ⁠י
5.note: Here, the word **to** marks the clause **to return Jacob to him** and **that Israel would be assembled to him** as the goal or purpose for which Yahweh formed the servant. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

6.note: Yahweh is using **It is too light for you to be** as a common expression of the culture to mean “it is too small a thing for you to only be.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is too small a thing for you to only be]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Isaiah as if he were **a light of the nations**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as someone who reveals truth to the nations]

Here, the connector **that** marks the clause **my salvation may be to the end of the earth** as the goal or purpose of the statement **I have given you as a light of the nations**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [that all of mankind may be saved]

Yahweh is using **to the end of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to the most distant places in the world.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the most distant places in the world]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my saving acts]

7.note: Some ancient manuscripts read “to the despiser of life, to the detester of the nation.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “to one despised in life, to one abhorred by the nation.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [princes will see and arise and prostrate themselves]

8.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **favor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my good pleasure]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [saving you]

Here, the word **to** marks the clause **to raise up the land** as the goal or purpose of the statement **I will give you as a covenant of the people**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

9.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֤ר לַֽ⁠אֲסוּרִים֙ צֵ֔אוּ לַ⁠אֲשֶׁ֥ר בַּ⁠חֹ֖שֶׁךְ הִגָּל֑וּ
9.note: Here, the word **to** marks the clause **to say to the prisoners** and what follows as a continuation (from the previous verse) of the goal or purpose for which Yahweh gives the servant as a covenant of the people. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.

Here Yahweh is speaking of his people as if they were a flock of sheep, saying that **they will graze** and that the bare heights will be **their pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [As they travel, they will find food, and even places that look barren will feed them]

10.note: This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **hunger**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [They will have enough to eat]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **thirst**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and they will be satisfied with water]

Yahweh is speaking of **the glaring heat and the sun** as if they were living things that could **strike** people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will not be harmed by the glaring heat or the sun]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one who cares deeply for them]

11.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of removing every obstacle to his people’s journey as if he would **make all of my mountains into a road**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will remove every obstacle from my people’s path]

12.note: The location of this place is uncertain, but it may refer to a region in the southern part of Egypt.

13.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

13.q: רָנּ֤וּ שָׁמַ֨יִם֙ וְ⁠גִ֣ילִי אָ֔רֶץ יפצחו הָרִ֖ים רִנָּ֑ה
13.note: Isaiah is speaking to the **heavens**, **earth**, and **mountains**, even though he knows they cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about Yahweh comforting his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about the heavens, earth, and mountains. Alternate translation: [The heavens should shout joyfully, the earth should rejoice, and the mountains should break forth into singing!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he will help his afflicted]

Isaiah is using the adjective **afflicted** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and he will have compassion on his afflicted people]

14.note: Isaiah is speaking of **Zion**, the city of Jerusalem, as if it were a living thing that could speak. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But the people living in Zion say]

15.q: הֲ⁠תִשְׁכַּ֤ח אִשָּׁה֙ עוּלָ֔⁠הּ מֵ⁠רַחֵ֖ם בֶּן בִּטְנָ֑⁠הּ
15.note: Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that it is unthinkable for a mother to forget her own child. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [A woman would never forget her nursing child, or stop having compassion on the son of her womb!]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **compassion**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from caring tenderly for the son of her womb]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will not forget** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his promise to his people. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, will not forget you]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **forget**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [I will surely remember you]

16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of remembering Zion permanently as if she were something he had inscribed on his hands, saying **on my palms I have inscribed you**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will never forget you]

In verses 16-23, the word **you** is feminine singular because it refers to Zion, which is being personified as a woman. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction, and use the feminine form if your language marks that distinction.
Here, **your walls** represents “your city.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your people]

17.note: Yahweh speaks of the people who are returning to live in Jerusalem as if they were the city’s children. Alternate translation: [Your inhabitants are hurrying back]

18.note: Yahweh is using **Lift up your eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “look up” or “look around.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Look up and]

The expression **they are gathered** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they have gathered together]
Following the custom of his culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something that he holds sacred. Alternate translation: [I swear by my own life]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who is speaking, **the declaration of Yahweh**, before the oath itself, **The life of me**. Alternate translation: [This is the declaration of Yahweh: The life of me, if]

The point of this comparison is that just as **jewelry** beautifies the person who wears it, so will **all of them**, the returning people, beautify Zion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [you do not wear all of them as adornment that beautifies you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a bride** adorns herself with ornaments, so Zion will **bind them on**, keeping the returning people as her adornment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and bind them on as a bride adorns herself with ornaments]

19.note: The words**devastation** and **desolation** mean basically the same thing and emphasize that the enemy has destroyed Zion and left it empty. Alternate translation: [Though you were completely desolate]
The enemy destroying Zion is spoken of as if they had devoured it. Alternate translation: [those who destroyed you]

20.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **sons** who are characterized by being born in a time of **bereavements**, that is, children born to a woman after she had lost other children. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the sons born to you after you lost other children]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people who will repopulate Zion as if they were **the sons of your bereavements**, children born to her after she had lost her earlier children. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the children born to you after your bereavement]

The word “you” s feminine singular everywhere else in verses 16-23 because Yahweh is addressing Zion (verse 14), using that city to represent the Judeans. But here the understood “you” in the imperative **draw near** is masculine singular because Yahweh is addressing a representative resident of the city. So use the masculine form if your language marks that distinction.

21.q: וְ⁠אָמַ֣רְתְּ בִּ⁠לְבָבֵ֗⁠ךְ מִ֤י יָֽלַד לִ⁠י֙ אֶת אֵ֔לֶּה
21.note: The term **say** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The expression **having been turned aside** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and with others having turned me aside]

Zion is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I was left** already includes this meaning. She is doing that to emphasize how utterly alone she was left. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I was indeed left by myself]

The expression **I was left by myself** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [everyone left me alone]

22.note: The term **says** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

22.q: אֶשָּׂ֤א אֶל־גּוֹיִם֙ יָדִ֔⁠י וְ⁠אֶל־עַמִּ֖ים אָרִ֣ים נִסִּ֑⁠י
22.note: Lifting up the hand and raising a banner was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that he was summoning the nations to act. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [I will summon the nations, and I will signal with my banner to the peoples]

22.q: אֶשָּׂ֤א אֶל גּוֹיִם֙ יָדִ֔⁠י וְ⁠אֶל עַמִּ֖ים אָרִ֣ים נִסִּ֑⁠י
22.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of summoning the nations as if he would **lift up my hand to the nations** and **raise my banner to the peoples**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will summon the nations, and I will signal to the peoples]

The expression **your daughters will be carried** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and the nations will carry your daughters on their shoulders]

23.note: Yahweh is using **Nostrils to the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “bowing down with the face to the ground.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They will bow down with their faces to the ground]

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [they will bow all the way down to the ground before you to show you great honor]

Yahweh is using **lick the dust of your feet** as a common expression of the culture to mean “show complete submission to you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will completely submit to you]

24.q: הֲ⁠יֻקַּ֥ח מִ⁠גִּבּ֖וֹר מַלְק֑וֹחַ וְ⁠אִם שְׁבִ֥י צַדִּ֖יק יִמָּלֵֽט
24.note: Isaiah is using the question form to express that this seems impossible. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The spoil cannot be taken from a warrior, nor can the captive of the righteous be rescued.]

The expression **the spoil be taken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Can anyone take the spoil from a warrior]

The expression **the captive of the righteous will be rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone will rescue the captive of the righteous]

Isaiah is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the righteous person]

Some ancient manuscripts read “the righteous.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “the terrible,” as in the next verse. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

25.note: The term **says** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

The expression **the captive of a warrior will be taken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will take the captive of a warrior]

The expression **the spoil of the terrible will be rescued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will rescue the spoil of the terrible]

Yahweh is using the adjective **terrible** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [and the spoil of the terrible one]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will contend** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself, and no one else, is the one who will fight against those who oppose his people. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I am the one who will contend with the one who contends with you]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will save** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who will rescue Zion’s children, in contrast to any human warrior. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and I myself will save your sons]

26.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of causing the oppressors to destroy one another as if he would **make your oppressors eat their flesh**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will cause your oppressors to destroy one another]

The point of this comparison is that just as **new wine** makes people drunk, so the oppressors will be overwhelmed by **their blood** that is shed. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and they will become drunk with their blood just as new wine makes people drunk]
Here, **all flesh** represents “all people.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all people]

Here, **Jacob** represents “the descendants of Jacob,” the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the Mighty One of the descendants of Jacob]
